title: Towards verifiable quantum advantage with random circuits: Observables that survive concentration
authors: Antonio A. Mele, Francesco A. Mele, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas E. O'Brien
abstract: Demonstrating quantum advantage on current quantum hardware is a central goal of quantum computing, and random quantum circuits underpin many leading proposals. Yet sampling-based demonstrations are often difficult to verify, while observable-based approaches face a different challenge: concentration can suppress differences between circuit instances. Recent experiments have put forward the estimation of out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) in random circuits as a promising task for verifiable quantum advantage, yet whether their circuit-to-circuit fluctuations survive concentration as system size grows has remained open. Here we show that they do. For broad classes of local random circuits in any fixed spatial dimension, we prove inverse-polynomial fluctuations of fixed-order OTOCs at system-scale depths. In one-dimensional Haar-random brickwork circuits, we further show that macroscopically many gates contribute to these fluctuations, yet in each layer they remain confined to a sublinear-width region. As a byproduct, we develop a classical algorithm exhibiting the first rigorous improvement over brute-force classical simulation of OTOCs in 1D. Although classical hardness remains open, our results rule out strong concentration as an obstruction to OTOC-based proposals for verifiable quantum advantage.
summary: This paper proves that Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) in random quantum circuits retain significant, measurable fluctuations as system size grows, thus providing a pathway for verifiable quantum advantage. The authors develop theoretical bounds and a novel classical algorithm to estimate these OTOCs efficiently by exploiting the localization of gate contributions within the circuit structure.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of verifying quantum advantage using observable measurements in random quantum circuits, specifically overcoming the issue of observable concentration.
main_result: They prove that fixed-order Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) exhibit inverse-polynomial circuit-to-circuit fluctuations at system-scale depths for local random circuits.
method: The authors use theoretical proofs based on relating the change in ensemble-averaged OTOC to lower bounds on the circuit-to-circuit variance, and develop a classical algorithm for efficient estimation.
model_or_system: The model involves local random quantum circuits, specifically analyzed using 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits acting on $n$ qubits.
key_observables: Out-of-time-order correlators ($	ext{OTOC}(k)$), particularly $	ext{OTOC}(1)$ and the infinite-temperature endpoint OTOC ($	ext{OTOC}_\infty$).
important_parameters: Fixed order $k$, system size $n$, and circuit depth $d$. The fluctuations are most visible in a depth window of $O(\sqrt{n})$ around $d^*=5n/3$ in 1D.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on bounding the error introduced by separating gates into a 'retained' region ($E_R$) and a 'random' region, and assumes the OTOC can be approximated by a conditional mean.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the depth dependence of $	ext{OTOC}(k)$ showing the transition from constant values to fluctuating regimes, and detail the geometry of the influential 'eye-shaped region' of gates.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general theorem on inverse-polynomial fluctuations. It then applies this to 1D circuits, deriving specific variance bounds ($\Omega(n^{-1/2})$) and developing a classical algorithm to estimate the OTOC at the critical depth by restricting the calculation to the localized 'eye-shaped region'.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous theoretical guarantees about the robustness of OTOC measurements against circuit randomness, which is crucial for designing verifiable quantum advantage experiments on near-term hardware.

At intermediate depths, circuit-to-circuit fluctuations become visible, before the observable approaches its deep-circuit behavior. The data show OTOC(2) ρ for ρ = |0n⟩⟨0n| in a one-dimensional open- boundary Haar-random brickwork circuit with n = 18 qubits, B = Z4, and M = Z14. For the infinite-temperature trace OTOC (left), only gates in the causal diamond LC− T (B) ∩LC+ T (M) can affect the observable.
